questions.question: A file has `import Data.List` written after a helper function's definition. What happens?
options: A parse error — imports must appear before any function definition, so they belong at the top of the file
It compiles fine; Haskell scans the whole file for imports before running anything
Only the functions defined after the import can use Data.List; earlier ones cannot
It works, but GHC prints a style warning
questions.explanation: This lesson states the rule directly: imports must appear before any function definition, so in practice they go at the top of the file. Writing one after a definition triggers a parse error, not a warning or a partial success.
optionFeedback: Correct — this is exactly the placement rule this lesson gives, and violating it is a parse error, listed again in this page's Common Errors table.
There is no such whole-file prescan; the placement rule is fixed and a misplaced import is rejected as a parse error.
Haskell import scope is not divided by position within the file relative to individual function definitions in this way — the real outcome is a parse error before any function runs at all.
This is a hard error, not a style warning — the file fails to compile at all until every import is moved above the definitions.

questions.question: import MyCalculator, with no parentheses and no hiding. What does this bring into scope?
options: Everything MyCalculator exports
Only the function named MyCalculator
Nothing, until a specific name is also written
Only the names MyCalculator shares with Prelude
questions.explanation: The plain form import ModuleName brings in everything the module exports — no parentheses to select particular names, no hiding to exclude any. Selective and hiding forms are separate syntax covered later in this lesson.
optionFeedback: Correct — the basic, unqualified, unrestricted form brings in the module's whole export list.
MyCalculator is the module's name, not a function inside it; this form imports everything the module exports, not a single same-named function.
Nothing extra needs to be written for the basic form to work; it is complete as written, unlike a selective import which does require naming what you want.
This form has nothing to do with what Prelude happens to export; it brings in everything MyCalculator itself exports, full stop.

questions.question: After `import Data.Char (toLower, toUpper)`, is `isDigit` available?
options: Yes, because it is imported alongside toLower and toUpper automatically
No — only the names listed in parentheses are brought into scope
Yes, because Data.Char is imported as a whole
It depends on whether Prelude also exports isDigit
questions.explanation: A selective import brings in exactly the names listed and nothing else. isDigit would need its own entry in the parentheses, or a separate unqualified import of Data.Char, to be usable.
optionFeedback: Selective imports do not pull in related functions automatically — only the exact names written in the parentheses come into scope.
Correct — import Data.Char (toLower, toUpper) brings in only toLower and toUpper. isDigit is not in scope without being listed too.
The whole module is not imported here — only the two names inside the parentheses were selected.
Whether Prelude happens to export something with the same name is a separate question; the issue is that isDigit was never selected from Data.Char.

questions.question: What does `import Data.List hiding (nub, sort)` bring into scope?
options: Only nub and sort
Nothing — hiding excludes everything
Everything Data.List exports except nub and sort
Everything, including nub and sort, with a warning
questions.explanation: hiding excludes exactly the names listed and imports everything else the module exports unqualified. Here, every Data.List function except nub and sort becomes available.
optionFeedback: That is the opposite of hiding's effect — a selective import (f, g) would bring in only those names; hiding excludes them instead.
hiding does not exclude the whole module — only the listed names are left out; everything else still comes in.
Correct — hiding (nub, sort) imports the rest of Data.List's exports, leaving out exactly the two named functions.
Excluded names are genuinely out of scope, not just discouraged with a warning; using nub afterwards would be a 'Variable not in scope' error.

questions.question: You have written your own `nub`. Which import lets you use it alongside the rest of Data.List?
options: import Data.List (nub)
import Data.List hiding (nub)
import Data.List as nub
import hiding Data.List (nub)
questions.explanation: hiding (nub) imports everything from Data.List except nub, leaving your own nub as the only one in scope under that name — with the rest of Data.List still available unqualified.
optionFeedback: This imports Data.List's nub specifically, which would clash with your own definition of the same name.
Correct — hiding (nub) excludes only Data.List's nub, so your own definition is the one that resolves.
as introduces an alias for the whole module (covered next), not a selection or exclusion of one name; this is not valid for this purpose.
hiding is written after the module name, not before it: import Data.List hiding (nub) is the correct order.

questions.question: Both Data.Map and Prelude define a function called filter. What happens with `import qualified Data.Map as Map` alongside the automatic Prelude import?
options: A compile error, because filter is ambiguous
Map.filter refers to Data.Map's version; filter alone still refers to Prelude's
Prelude's filter is silently replaced
Both filters merge into one overloaded function
questions.explanation: Because Data.Map was imported qualified, none of its names enter scope unprefixed — only Map.filter, Map.insert, and so on do. filter written alone is therefore unambiguous: it can only mean Prelude's, since Data.Map's filter was never brought into scope under that bare name.
optionFeedback: There is no ambiguity here precisely because the import was qualified — Data.Map's names all require the Map. prefix, so the bare name filter has only one meaning.
Correct — qualified imports never introduce their names unprefixed, so filter unprefixed still means Prelude's, while Map.filter reaches Data.Map's.
Prelude's filter remains exactly as it was; qualified importing does not touch or shadow it.
Haskell has no mechanism that merges two same-named functions into one; you always call one specific version, selected by whether you use the prefix.

questions.question: `import qualified Data.Map as Map` and `import qualified Data.Set as Map` appear in the same file. What happens?
options: Both are accepted; Map. resolves based on argument types
An error, because the alias Map cannot name two different modules at once
The second import silently overrides the first
Haskell merges Data.Map and Data.Set into one namespace called Map
questions.explanation: Rule from this lesson: several modules may share an alias only 'as long as there are no conflicting items.' Data.Map and Data.Set both export names like insert and empty, so aliasing both to Map creates exactly the conflict the rule warns about, and GHC rejects it.
optionFeedback: Haskell does not resolve names by argument type at the module level; an alias names one module (or a compatible group with no clashes), not a type-directed dispatcher.
Correct — Data.Map and Data.Set both export overlapping names such as insert, so sharing the alias Map produces an ambiguous-name conflict.
Both import statements are processed; neither silently disappears — the conflict is reported instead.
The two modules remain entirely separate; only the shared alias text is affected, and it is exactly that sharing which causes the error here.

questions.question: Why is `Map.lookup "Sipho" marks` written with the `Map.` prefix rather than plain `lookup`?
options: Map.lookup and lookup are different operations entirely
Data.Map was imported qualified, so its names are only reachable through the Map. prefix
lookup does not exist in Data.Map
The prefix is optional style, not a requirement
questions.explanation: import qualified Data.Map as Map brings in every Data.Map name, but only accessible via Map.name. Prelude's own lookup :: Eq a => a -> [(a, b)] -> Maybe b works on association lists, a different data structure, so keeping the two separate under different names is exactly the point of the qualified import.
optionFeedback: They serve a closely related purpose (looking a key up) — Data.Map's version is simply written for the Map type instead of an association list, and both return Maybe.
Correct — a qualified import never introduces its names unprefixed, so Map.lookup is the only way to reach Data.Map's version.
Data.Map does export a function named lookup; it is simply not usable as bare lookup once imported qualified.
It is required here, not optional — without the prefix, GHC would look for an unqualified lookup, which Prelude's own version already claims.

questions.question: After `Map.insert "Sipho" 55 marks`, what is `marks` itself?
options: The original map, unchanged, with two entries
The updated map, now with three entries
Nothing — marks is deleted after the insert
An error, because marks was already defined
questions.explanation: Map.insert, like every Haskell update, returns a new map and leaves its argument untouched. Unless the result is given a new name and used, marks keeps its original two entries — the same immutability already seen with record update syntax.
optionFeedback: Correct — marks is never mutated. Map.insert produces a new map value; marks itself still has only Kago and Naledi.
That describes the return value of the expression, not marks itself. To keep the three-entry map you would bind the result to a new name.
Nothing is deleted; marks continues to exist exactly as it was defined.
Calling Map.insert with marks as an argument is completely ordinary and does not conflict with marks's earlier definition.

deeper-reasoning-choosing-the-right-form.title: Deeper reasoning: choosing the right form of import

questions.question: A student imports Data.Map and then wonders whether lookup in their program means the Prelude's list lookup or the map's lookup. A classmate suggests a qualified import. Which explanation of the two lookups in the program below, and of why the qualified form is the right tool, is the most accurate?
options: The two lookups are the same function, so the qualification is only decoration, and the program prints Just "one" twice.

A qualified import requires every name from that module to carry its module prefix, so Map.lookup is unambiguously the map's version and plain lookup is still the Prelude's. The program prints Just "one" and Just "uno". Without qualifying, importing Data.Map would bring in a second lookup and make the unqualified name ambiguous. The alias Map is just a shorter prefix for the module, and as does not by itself change what is imported.
The program does not compile, because Haskell allows only one function named lookup in a program.
The first line prints Nothing, because maps start out empty and Map.insert does not change them.
questions.explanation: Qualified imports keep the origin of every name visible. They are the standard remedy when two modules export the same name, and an alias keeps the prefix short.
optionFeedback: The two functions work on different structures and have different types. They give different results here.
Correct. The prefix says exactly which module each name comes from, and the alias is a convenience.
Different modules may define functions with the same name. Qualified names keep them apart.
Map.insert returns a new map containing the key, so the lookup finds it. Maps are immutable, but the inserted version is the one that is used.

questions.question: A student writes tally with a selective import and later adds a call to nub inside it, which GHC reports as not in scope. They protest: "I imported Data.List, so everything in it should be available." Which explanation is correct, and which repair best fits the intention?
code: tally xs = map (\g -> (head g, length g)) (group (sort xs))
options: Selective imports are ignored by GHC, so nub must have been spelled incorrectly.

A selective import brings in only the names in its list, here sort and group, so nub is not in scope. That is the point of the form: it documents exactly what the module depends on and prevents unexpected clashes. The repair is to add nub to the list, or to import the module in full if most of it is needed. An import cannot combine a list of wanted names with a hiding clause; it is either one or the other.
The repair is to write nub twice, because every imported name must be listed twice.
The repair is to put the import after the definition of tally, because imports are read from the bottom of the file.
questions.explanation: The list in a selective import is a complete statement of what is imported. Anything not listed is absent, which is helpful when reading the file and when avoiding clashes, but it means each new dependency must be listed.
optionFeedback: GHC honours the list exactly, which is why the unlisted name is missing.
Correct. The cost and the benefit of a selective import come from the same property: only what is listed is visible.
There is no need to repeat names in an import list.
Imports must come before the definitions in a file, not after them.

questions.question: A student has written their own nub and also wants the rest of Data.List. They write the first version below and it works. A classmate removes the hiding clause and the program stops compiling with an ambiguity error. Which explanation is correct?
options: Removing hiding fixes a warning, so the program compiles and prints [1,2,3] in both versions.

Without hiding, the import brings in Data.List's own nub, so the name nub refers to two different functions, the library one and the local definition, and GHC reports an ambiguous occurrence where it is used. hiding (nub) imports everything else from the module but not that name, which removes the clash. It applies to functions and values, not to types, and it cannot be combined with a selective list in the same import.
The ambiguity arises because Data.List is imported twice, so removing one import fixes it.
The ambiguity arises because hiding is required for every import that comes before a function definition.
questions.explanation: Two different entities with the same name in scope make an unqualified use ambiguous. hiding is one remedy, selective import is another, and qualified import is a third, depending on how much of the module is wanted.
optionFeedback: The version without hiding does not compile. GHC treats the clash as an error at the point of use.
Correct. The clash is between an imported and a local name, and hiding removes the imported one.
The module is imported only once in either version. The clash is about the name nub.
hiding is not required in general. It is only needed when a name would otherwise clash.
